led-display-001.question: Which correctly describes how a light-emitting diode (LED) emits light?
choices: Photons are emitted when electrons and holes are pulled apart by the strong field in a reverse-biased pn junction, releasing the energy they gain as light
Electrons and holes injected into the pn junction under forward bias recombine and emit photons with an energy close to the band gap
Only the active layer is heated locally by Joule heating as current flows, and the semiconductor crystal emits light as blackbody radiation, as in an incandescent bulb
led-display-001.explanation: When an LED is forward biased, electrons from the n side and holes from the p side are injected into the junction (usually a quantum-well active layer), where conduction-band electrons recombine with valence-band holes. The surplus energy is released as a photon roughly equal to the band gap Eg, so the emission wavelength is set by the material's Eg and the spectrum is narrow, a few tens of nm wide. Pulling electrons and holes apart under reverse bias to produce a current is how a photodiode receives light, the opposite direction. Glowing by heat as blackbody radiation is the principle of the incandescent bulb; an LED emits by electroluminescence while staying cool, and its efficiency actually falls as the active layer heats up.

led-display-002.question: What is the main reason silicon is hardly ever used as the active layer of visible or near-infrared LEDs?
choices: With a band gap of 1.12 eV, the energy released in recombination is not enough even for one near-infrared photon, so it cannot emit light at any wavelength
Even with doping, p-type and n-type regions cannot be made in the same silicon crystal, so electrons and holes cannot be injected into the same place through a pn junction
It is an indirect-gap semiconductor, so recombination needs a phonon to supply momentum; radiative recombination is unlikely and loses to nonradiative recombination
led-display-002.explanation: Silicon is an indirect-gap semiconductor in which the bottom of the conduction band and the top of the valence band sit at different wavevectors (momenta). A photon carries almost no momentum, so radiative recombination requires a phonon to take part at the same time, and its probability is orders of magnitude smaller than in direct-gap semiconductors such as GaAs and InGaN. Meanwhile, nonradiative recombination through defects takes place, so the emission efficiency is very low. A band gap of 1.12 eV corresponds to a near-infrared photon at about 1.1 µm, so the energy is not insufficient. Silicon is the material in which pn junctions are made freely for photodiodes and integrated circuits, so the claim that junctions cannot be formed is also wrong.

led-display-003.question: A blue LED with an internal quantum efficiency of 90% and a light-extraction efficiency of 80% is driven at 100 mA. Taking the efficiency with which electrons are injected into the active layer as 1, which is closest to the number of photons leaving the LED per second? (elementary charge q = 1.6×10⁻¹⁹ C)
choices: About 4.5×10¹⁷
About 6.3×10¹⁷
About 5.6×10¹⁷
led-display-003.explanation: The number of electrons flowing in per second is I/q = 0.1/(1.6×10⁻¹⁹) ≈ 6.25×10¹⁷. The external quantum efficiency is the product of the injection efficiency, the fraction that becomes photons in the active layer (internal quantum efficiency) and the fraction of photons that escape the device (light-extraction efficiency), here 1 × 0.9 × 0.8 = 0.72. So the photons leaving are 6.25×10¹⁷ × 0.72 ≈ 4.5×10¹⁷ per second. About 6.3×10¹⁷ forgets the efficiencies and assumes every electron always leaves as one photon. About 5.6×10¹⁷ applies only the internal quantum efficiency, counting photons that are absorbed or trapped inside the device.

led-display-004.question: A 450 nm blue LED driven at 3.0 V and 350 mA gives an optical output of 500 mW. Which pair is closest to the external quantum efficiency (photons emitted per electron) and the wall-plug efficiency (optical output / electrical input)? (photon energy E[eV] ≈ 1240/λ[nm])
choices: External quantum efficiency about 48%, wall-plug efficiency about 52%
Both the external quantum efficiency and the wall-plug efficiency about 48%
External quantum efficiency about 52%, wall-plug efficiency about 48%
led-display-004.explanation: One photon carries 1240/450 ≈ 2.76 eV, so the photon rate is 0.5 W/(2.76 × 1.6×10⁻¹⁹ J) and the electron rate is 0.35 A/q. Their ratio gives an external quantum efficiency of 0.5/(2.76 × 0.35) ≈ 0.52, about 52%. The wall-plug efficiency is 0.5/(3.0 × 0.35) ≈ 0.48, about 48%. The two differ by the ratio of the 2.76 eV leaving as a photon to the 3.0 eV each electron receives from the supply (about 0.92); the extra voltage across electrodes and semiconductor resistance is a loss. The choice with both equal overlooks this difference. The swapped pair confuses the definitions: the wall-plug efficiency can exceed the EQE only if the drive voltage is below 2.76 V.

led-display-005.question: Inside a GaN crystal with refractive index 2.5, light is emitted uniformly in all directions from one point. Which is closest to the fraction that can leave through one flat top face into air? Consider only total internal reflection at the top face and ignore Fresnel reflection and absorption.
choices: About 4%
About 8%
About 26%
led-display-005.explanation: Only light inside the cone within the critical angle θc = arcsin(1/2.5) ≈ 23.6° (the escape cone) can leave through the top face. The ratio of the cone's solid angle 2π(1 − cosθc) to the full 4π is (1 − cos23.6°)/2 ≈ 0.042, about 4%. For small angles this is approximated by 1/(4n²) = 0.04. About 8% forgets to divide by 2, taking the ratio to a hemisphere instead of the full sphere, and about 26% mistakes the angle ratio 23.6°/90° for the solid-angle ratio. The rest of the light is absorbed while bouncing by total internal reflection, so extraction is improved by surface roughening, patterned sapphire substrates, and encapsulation in resin with an index of about 1.5 (which widens the critical angle to about 36.9°).

led-display-006.question: In an InGaN blue LED, as the current density is raised, the external quantum efficiency peaks at a low current and then falls at high currents. Which correctly pairs this phenomenon with its main suspected causes?
choices: It is called efficiency droop; defect-assisted nonradiative recombination (SRH recombination) rises sharply at high current and takes most of the injected carriers
It is called efficiency droop; processes that produce no light, such as Auger recombination growing as the cube of carrier density and electron leakage from the active layer, increase at high current
It is called efficiency droop; the band gap of the active layer grows with current, so each photon carries more energy and fewer photons are emitted for the same power
led-display-006.explanation: The recombination rate is written as An + Bn² + Cn³ with carrier density n, where A is defect-assisted nonradiative recombination, B is radiative recombination and C is Auger recombination. The internal quantum efficiency is Bn²/(An + Bn² + Cn³), so at low current the defect term An is relatively large, and raising the current lets Bn² win and the efficiency rise. Raising it further brings in Auger recombination, which grows as n³, and leakage of electrons over the active layer into the p side, so the efficiency falls. This is efficiency droop, a problem when driving at high current for lighting. Defect recombination is proportional to n, so it becomes relatively smaller at high current. The idea that the band gap grows with current and changes the efficiency is also wrong.

led-display-007.question: Which change matches the general trend when the temperature of an LED's active layer (junction) rises? (The current is kept constant.)
choices: The band gap shrinks, so the emission wavelength shifts longer, and nonradiative recombination increases, so the optical output falls
The band gap widens, so the emission wavelength shifts shorter, and the optical output rises
The emission wavelength is fixed by the material and does not change; only the optical output falls
led-display-007.explanation: A semiconductor's band gap shrinks as temperature rises, through lattice expansion and electron-phonon interaction, so the emission peak shifts to longer wavelengths. Defect-assisted nonradiative recombination and carrier leakage from the active layer also increase with temperature, so the optical output falls at the same current. Red AlGaInP LEDs are especially temperature sensitive, and when combined with blue InGaN LEDs to make white light, the color can drift with temperature. The choice with shorter wavelength and higher output has the direction of the band-gap change reversed. The choice with an unchanged wavelength overlooks the temperature dependence of the band gap. This is why thermal design matters for lighting LEDs.

led-display-008.question: In a white LED, a phosphor absorbs part of the 450 nm blue light and converts it to 560 nm yellow light. If the phosphor's quantum yield (photons emitted per photon absorbed) is 0.9, which is closest to the fraction of the absorbed blue-light energy that comes out as yellow light?
choices: About 90%
About 80%
About 72%
led-display-008.explanation: A photon's energy is inversely proportional to its wavelength, so converting one 450 nm photon into one 560 nm photon multiplies its energy by 450/560 ≈ 0.80. This is the Stokes loss of the phosphor, and the remaining roughly 20% becomes heat. With a quantum yield of 0.9 on top of that, the energy conversion efficiency is 0.9 × 0.80 ≈ 0.72, about 72%. About 90% considers only the quantum yield and forgets the energy lost by the longer wavelength. About 80% conversely considers only the energy ratio per photon and forgets absorption that does not produce photons (the quantum yield). The energy lost in the phosphor heats it and reduces its efficiency and lifetime, so it must also be considered in the thermal design of white LEDs.

led-display-009.question: Which correctly describes a white LED that combines a blue LED with a yellow phosphor (YAG:Ce)?
choices: The phosphor converts part of the blue to yellow, which mixes with the transmitted blue and looks white. Adding a red phosphor supplies the missing red and raises both color rendering and luminous efficacy
The phosphor converts part of the blue to yellow, which mixes with the transmitted blue and looks white. Adding a red phosphor raises color rendering but tends to lower luminous efficacy
The phosphor converts all of the blue light to yellow, so only yellow light comes out, but yellow lies between red and green and therefore looks white
led-display-009.explanation: In this scheme part of the blue light passes through the phosphor and the rest is converted to broad light centered on yellow. Blue and yellow are complementary, so their mixture looks white. With little red, however, red objects are rendered poorly, and the color rendering index typically stays around 70 to 80. Adding a red phosphor raises color rendering, but it adds light beyond 600 nm where the eye is less sensitive, so the luminous flux per unit optical power drops and the luminous efficacy (lm/W) tends to fall. The choice where both rise overlooks this trade-off. If all the blue light were converted to yellow, the output would look yellow, not white.

led-display-010.question: In an organic light-emitting diode (OLED) using a conventional fluorescent material (one with no mechanism for converting triplet excitons to singlets), take the charge balance (the fraction of injected electrons and holes that form excitons) as 1, the quantum yield of light emission by excitons as 1, and the light-extraction efficiency as 20%. Taking into account the fraction of excitons formed as set by spin statistics, which is closest to the upper limit of the external quantum efficiency?
choices: About 5%
About 20%
About 15%
led-display-010.explanation: Excitons formed when electrons and holes recombine are created as 25% singlets and 75% triplets because of the possible spin combinations. In a fluorescent material only singlets can emit light, so the internal quantum efficiency is limited to 25%. Multiplying by the 20% light-extraction efficiency gives an upper limit for the external quantum efficiency of 0.25 × 0.2 = 0.05, about 5%. About 20% is the limit for phosphorescent materials (complexes containing heavy atoms such as iridium), which can emit from triplets as well, and does not apply to fluorescent materials. About 15% swaps the singlet and triplet fractions, assuming 75% emit. Materials that thermally convert triplets back to singlets (TADF) exceed this limit. The light-extraction efficiency of OLEDs is as low as about 20% because light is trapped in the high-index organic layers, transparent electrode and glass.

led-display-011.question: Which correctly describes a feature of an OLED display compared with a liquid-crystal display (LCD)?
choices: The pixels emit light themselves, but black is shown by blocking backlight with liquid crystal, so black is slightly raised
The pixels emit light themselves, so a pixel showing black only needs to stop emitting, and the contrast in a dark room can be made extremely high
The pixels do not emit light themselves, so a strong backlight is needed to show a bright white
led-display-011.explanation: An OLED is self-emissive: the organic layer of each pixel glows with current, so a pixel showing black does not emit if no current flows. Apart from reflected ambient light, the black luminance can be nearly zero, and the contrast ratio in a dark environment becomes very high. In an LCD the liquid crystal does not emit light; it is an optical shutter that passes or blocks backlight with polarizers and liquid crystal. Some light leaks even when showing black, the contrast ratio is roughly several hundred to several thousand to one, and local dimming, which darkens the backlight region by region, is used to compensate. The choices about backlight leaking in black and needing a strong backlight both apply LCD properties to OLEDs. OLEDs, on the other hand, can suffer burn-in when the same image is shown for a long time.

led-display-012.question: A normally white liquid-crystal display places a 90° twisted nematic (TN) liquid crystal between two polarizers with crossed transmission axes. Which correctly describes the operation of a pixel?
choices: Without voltage, light is blocked; with voltage, the molecules twist by 90° and rotate the polarization, so light passes only when it lines up with the exit polarizer's transmission axis
The liquid crystal itself acts as a polarizer, so one polarizer is enough, and voltage changes the liquid crystal's absorption to set the brightness according to the twist angle
Without voltage, the polarization follows the 90° twist and light passes; with voltage, the molecules stand up along the field, the polarization no longer rotates, and light is blocked
led-display-012.explanation: In a TN liquid crystal, alignment layers on the two substrates arrange the molecules with a 90° twist. Without voltage, incoming linearly polarized light follows the twist of the molecules, changing direction as it travels, and comes out rotated by 90°. It then matches the transmission axis of the crossed exit polarizer and passes, so the pixel is white with no voltage (normally white). With voltage, the dielectric anisotropy makes the molecules stand up along the field, the rotation of polarization by the twist disappears, and the exit polarizer blocks the light, giving black. Intermediate voltages give intermediate brightness. Dark without voltage and bright with it is the normally black case with parallel polarizers, and even then voltage untwists the molecules rather than twisting them. Liquid crystal changes the polarization state and cannot replace a polarizer, so two polarizers are needed.

led-display-013.question: Estimate the transmittance of a liquid-crystal display from the unpolarized backlight to the screen. Take the transmittance of the two polarizers and liquid crystal together as 40% (for unpolarized input), that of the color filter as 30%, and the pixel aperture ratio (the fraction of area not blocked by wiring and transistors) as 60%. Which is closest to the overall transmittance for a white display?
choices: About 2.9%
About 24%
About 7.2%
led-display-013.explanation: Light passes through each stage in turn, so the transmittances are multiplied: 0.40 × 0.30 × 0.60 = 0.072, about 7.2%. Unpolarized light passing an absorbing polarizer is in principle reduced to half or less, and real polarizers and liquid crystal together give about 40%. A color filter passes only one of red, green and blue, so a single subpixel passes about a third or less of white light. About 2.9% multiplies the 40% for the two polarizers in a second time, counting that loss twice. About 24% forgets the color filter. Since more than 90% of the backlight is lost inside the panel, efficiency is raised with films that reflect and recycle the polarization the polarizer would discard and by improving the aperture ratio.

led-display-014.question: To widen a display's color gamut, the spectral widths of the red, green and blue primaries are narrowed (for example with quantum dots or narrow-band phosphors). Which is the correct reason?
choices: The narrower and more monochromatic the spectrum, the closer the primaries move to the spectral locus of the xy diagram, so the triangle with the three primaries as vertices expands outward
Narrowing the spectrum raises the primaries' luminance for the same power, and the triangle of the three primaries on the chromaticity diagram grows outward in proportion to the luminance
The wider the spectrum, the more wavelengths it contains, so more colors can be reproduced by mixing and the gamut widens
led-display-014.explanation: Colors reproducible by mixing three primaries are limited to the inside of the triangle on the xy chromaticity diagram whose vertices are the primaries' chromaticities. Monochromatic light lies on the horseshoe-shaped spectral locus, and broader light mixes in neighboring wavelengths and moves inward (toward white), becoming less saturated. Quantum dots let the emission wavelength be chosen by size and have narrow widths of a few tens of nm, so the primaries move toward the locus and the triangle widens. Chromaticity is a coordinate independent of brightness, so higher luminance does not change the triangle's size. The choice that a wider spectrum widens the gamut is backwards: the primaries lose saturation and the gamut narrows. Ideal monochromatic primaries give the widest gamut, and the BT.2020 primaries lie on the spectral locus.

led-display-015.question: An image made for sRGB is shown as is, without color conversion (color management), on a display whose gamut is wider than sRGB. How does it look?
choices: Because the display's gamut contains sRGB, the sRGB image is automatically shown in its correct colors with nothing out of range
The display's primaries lie outside the sRGB primaries on the chromaticity diagram, so the same RGB values look too vivid
Because the display's primaries lie further out, the same RGB values are spread over a wider gamut and diluted, so the sRGB image looks dull
led-display-015.explanation: RGB values say how strongly to mix each primary, and the resulting color is set by the primaries' chromaticities. The red (255, 0, 0) in sRGB means the sRGB red primary, but on a wide-gamut display shown as is, the display's red primary, which lies further out, lights up and the red becomes more vivid than intended. Skin tones and everything else also gain saturation and look unnatural. Correct display requires converting the values from the image's color space to the display's, so that colors within sRGB are output at sRGB chromaticities. A wider gamut alone does not give correct colors automatically. Looking dull is the opposite case, which happens when wide-gamut image values are shown as is on a display with a narrower gamut.

led-display-016.question: The full width at half maximum of the spontaneous emission spectrum of an ideal LED is about 1.8kT in energy, where k is Boltzmann's constant and T the temperature. For a GaAs LED emitting at a center wavelength of 870 nm at 300 K (kT = 0.0259 eV), which value is closest to the FWHM expressed in wavelength? Use E[eV] ≈ 1240/λ[nm].
choices: About 28 nm
About 16 nm
About 8 nm
led-display-016.explanation: The energy width is 1.8 × 0.0259 ≈ 0.047 eV. From E = 1240/λ, Δλ ≈ λ²ΔE/1240 = 870² × 0.047/1240 ≈ 28 nm. About 16 nm takes the width as kT, and about 8 nm as kT/2; neither uses the factor 1.8. Electrons and holes are thermally distributed within their bands, spreading over several kT in energy, so LED light is not sharp like a laser line but has a width of tens of nanometers. For the same energy width, Δλ scales as λ², so longer-wavelength LEDs have wider spectra in wavelength terms.

led-display-017.question: An LED chip is sometimes encapsulated in a hemisphere of transparent resin with a refractive index of about 1.5, with the chip near the center of the hemisphere. Which statement correctly explains why this raises the light extraction efficiency?
choices: The resin index lies between those of air and the chip, so the critical angle at the resin surface becomes smaller, making light reflect many times inside the hemisphere before being concentrated toward the front

The critical angle from chip to resin is larger than to air, so more light leaves the chip, and light meets the hemispherical surface nearly normally, so it is not totally reflected on leaving the resin
The lens action of the hemisphere brings the light to a focus, which eliminates total internal reflection inside the chip, so all the light is extracted regardless of the chip's refractive index
led-display-017.explanation: Going directly from the semiconductor chip (index 2.5–3.5) into air, the critical angle is small and only light within a narrow cone escapes. With resin of index 1.5 in contact, the critical angle widens to sin⁻¹(1.5/n), so more light leaves the chip into the resin. Making the resin surface a hemisphere with the chip at its center means light from the center strikes the surface almost normally and passes from resin to air without total reflection. A flat resin layer would instead cause total reflection at the resin-air interface, so the shape matters. Trapping light at the resin surface would not raise the extraction, and some light is still totally reflected inside the chip, so not all of it can be extracted.

led-display-018.question: A white LED has a luminous efficacy of radiation (luminous flux per watt of emitted optical power) of 320 lm/W and a wall-plug efficiency (optical output power / electrical input) of 40%. Which value is closest to the luminous flux per watt of electrical input (the luminous efficacy of the source)?
choices: About 270 lm/W
About 800 lm/W
About 130 lm/W
led-display-018.explanation: The source efficacy is the product of the electrical-to-optical power conversion efficiency and the efficacy of radiation set by the spectrum: 0.40 × 320 lm/W = 128 lm/W, about 130 lm/W. About 270 lm/W multiplies the efficiency by the maximum luminous efficacy of 683 lm/W, which applies only to monochromatic light at 555 nm, ignoring the spectral weighting of white light. About 800 lm/W wrongly divides by the efficiency; no light source can exceed 683 lm/W. The efficacy of radiation is set by the weighting of the luminosity function V(λ) and is around 300 lm/W for white light containing blue and red components. Adding deep-red components to raise color rendering lowers this value.

led-display-019.question: Which is the main reason that IPS (in-plane switching) liquid-crystal displays have a wider viewing angle than TN displays?
choices: A lateral electric field parallel to the substrates rotates the molecules within the plane, so they do not tilt up, and the birefringence seen by light changes little even when viewed obliquely
An electric field perpendicular to the substrates stands the molecules up, so from oblique angles, just as from the front, their orientation lines up with the direction in which the light travels
It switches light by liquid-crystal scattering alone, without polarizers, so there is no polarization-related angular dependence and the image looks equally bright from every direction
led-display-019.explanation: In a TN cell, applying a voltage tilts the molecules up from the substrates. Tilted molecules present very different angles to light depending on the viewing direction, so oblique viewing changes the polarization effect of the birefringence, altering brightness and color and sometimes even inverting gray levels. An IPS cell applies a field parallel to the substrates from electrodes on one substrate, rotating the molecules within the plane to control polarization. The molecules stay lying down and only change direction, so the birefringence varies little with viewing angle and the viewing angle is wide. Standing molecules up with a perpendicular field is how TN and VA cells work, and the molecules align with the light path for only one direction, straight on. IPS also uses two polarizers and is not a scattering-type display.

led-display-020.question: The external quantum efficiency of LEDs is high in the blue and red but tends to be low in the green to yellow-green around 550 nm (the green gap). Which explanation of the main causes is correct?
choices: The eye's luminosity function is lowest near 550 nm, so even when emitting the same number of photons, green LEDs are measured as dimmer and their external quantum efficiency appears low
In InGaN, raising the In content lowers efficiency through effects such as electron-hole separation by internal fields, while AlGaInP approaches an indirect band gap as its wavelength is shortened
The energy of green photons exceeds the band gap of the active layer, so the light is strongly absorbed in the active layer and lost before it can escape
led-display-020.explanation: To shift the emission of InGaN, used for blue LEDs, to longer wavelengths, the In fraction is increased. More In increases the strain, and the resulting piezoelectric field pulls electrons and holes to opposite sides of the well (the quantum-confined Stark effect), lowering the recombination probability; compositional fluctuations and defects also contribute, and the size of each contribution is still being studied. In AlGaInP, used for red LEDs, adding Al to shorten the wavelength brings the conduction-band minimum close to an indirect valley, and electrons escape there or into the p side, lowering efficiency. Green falls between the two material systems, so efficiency suffers there. The luminosity function actually peaks near 555 nm, and external quantum efficiency is a ratio of photon numbers that does not involve it. The active layer emits photons near its band-gap energy, not above it.

led-display-021.question: In micro-LEDs with pixel sizes of a few to a few tens of µm, the external quantum efficiency tends to fall as the chip is made smaller. Which is the main reason?
choices: A smaller chip lowers the current density at the same current, which strengthens efficiency droop and increases non-radiative Auger recombination
The smaller the chip, the narrower the critical angle from the crystal to air, so a larger share of light is trapped inside by total internal reflection and absorbed
Non-radiative surface recombination at defects on the etched sidewalls grows relatively larger as the ratio of perimeter to area increases
led-display-021.explanation: Etching that separates the chips leaves crystal damage and dangling bonds on the sidewalls, and carriers reaching them recombine without emitting light. Chip area scales with the square of the size and the perimeter with its first power, so the smaller the chip, the larger the relative effect of the sidewalls, and efficiency drops sharply especially in materials with long carrier diffusion lengths. Sidewall passivation is therefore important. Efficiency droop occurs at high current density, so blaming a lower current density gets the direction backwards. The critical angle is set by the index ratio and does not depend on chip size.

led-display-022.question: In some LCDs the backlight is built from mini-LEDs divided into hundreds to thousands of zones, and the zones behind dark parts of the image are dimmed (local dimming). Which combination of effect and drawback is correct?
choices: Light leaves without passing through the liquid crystal and polarizers, so their losses disappear and power consumption falls greatly, but the liquid-crystal response slows in proportion to the number of zones
Less light leaks through black pixels, so contrast rises greatly, but zones around bright objects also light up, and faint glowing halos tend to appear on dark backgrounds
Each zone can change LED color, so colors can be shown without color filters, and the larger pixel aperture that results also raises the resolution
led-display-022.explanation: A liquid crystal blocks light by controlling polarization with voltage, but even in black a little light leaks through the polarizers and liquid crystal, so with a uniformly lit backlight the black looks gray and the contrast ratio stays at roughly one to several thousand to one. Local dimming darkens the LEDs in the dark zones, so the leaked light itself falls, the blacks deepen and contrast rises sharply. Zones are much larger than pixels, though, so a zone containing a bright object and its neighbors light up, and halos can appear on a dark background. The liquid crystal and polarizers remain in the light path, so their losses do not disappear. Color still comes from the color filters, so per-zone color control does not raise resolution.

led-display-023.question: A display with a white luminance of 400 cd/m² and a black luminance of 1 cd/m² is used in a bright room, where ambient light reflected from the screen surface adds 4 cd/m² to both white and black. Which value is closest to the contrast ratio (white luminance/black luminance) in this condition?
choices: About 81:1
About 100:1
About 400:1
led-display-023.explanation: Reflected light adds equally to white and black, so the contrast ratio is (400 + 4)/(1 + 4) = 404/5 ≈ 81. About 400:1 is the dark-room value and ignores the reflection. About 100:1 divides the white luminance by the reflected luminance alone and drops the black luminance itself. Even if the black luminance is lowered for a large dark-room contrast ratio, in a bright room the reflection sets the black and the ratio falls sharply. That is why anti-reflection treatment of the screen and polarizers that absorb ambient light largely decide how readable a display is in bright places.

led-display-024.question: Quantum dots (semiconductor particles a few nm across, such as CdSe or InP) are used as color-conversion materials that turn blue light into green or red. Which correctly describes the relation between particle size and emission color?
choices: The smaller the particle, the more the electron and hole spread out, the narrower the level spacing, and the longer (redder) the emission wavelength
The emission color is set only by the band gap of the material; particle size affects only the brightness and lifetime of the emission
The smaller the particle, the wider the level spacing from confinement and the shorter (bluer) the emission wavelength; the same material can give green or red by choosing the size
led-display-024.explanation: When a particle shrinks to about the size of the electron and hole wave extent (the Bohr radius), quantum confinement makes the energy levels discrete and raises the effective band gap above the bulk value. The smaller the particle, the stronger this effect and the shorter the emission wavelength. In CdSe, for example, small particles emit green and larger ones red. Particles of uniform size give a narrow emission spectrum, which widens a display's color gamut. Saying smaller particles emit redder reverses the effect of confinement. Saying color is set by the material alone overlooks the change due to confinement.

led-display-025.question: When the brightness of an InGaN green LED is adjusted by changing its current, the emission peak can shift to shorter wavelengths as the current increases. Which combination of the main reason and a method to adjust brightness without changing color is correct?
choices: More current lowers the junction temperature and widens the band gap; dimming by varying the current continuously keeps the junction temperature constant, so the color does not change
Injected carriers screen the internal field in the wells and weaken the quantum-confined Stark effect; PWM dimming, varying the on-time fraction at a fixed current, is used
More current makes high-energy electrons from Auger recombination emit light; adding a series resistor to cap the current keeps the color from changing
led-display-025.explanation: InGaN quantum wells carry a large strain-induced piezoelectric field that tilts the bands and lowers the emission energy (the quantum-confined Stark effect). Raising the current lets carriers in the wells screen this field, reducing the tilt, and band filling adds to it, so the emission peak shifts to shorter wavelengths. The effect is large in indium-rich green LEDs. To keep the color while changing brightness, PWM dimming is used, blinking the LED rapidly at a fixed current and varying the on-time fraction. More current actually raises the junction temperature, which narrows the band gap and shifts the emission to longer wavelengths. A series resistor only sets the current and cannot prevent the current-dependent color shift.

led-display-026.question: Assume the emission from a flat-faced LED chip is Lambertian (luminous intensity proportional to cosθ, where θ is the angle from the normal). Roughly what percentage of the total flux emitted into the forward hemisphere falls within a cone of ±30° about the normal? (The fraction within a cone of half-angle θ is sin²θ.)
choices: About 33%
About 13%
About 25%
led-display-026.explanation: When the intensity is proportional to cosθ, the flux inside a cone of half-angle θ is proportional to sin²θ, which reaches 1 for the whole hemisphere (θ = 90°). Since sin²30° = 0.25, about 25% of the total flux falls within ±30°. About 13% assumes uniform intensity and uses the solid-angle fraction 1 − cos30° ≈ 0.134, ignoring that the emission is strongest straight ahead. About 33% uses the angle ratio 30°/90° directly. Although the source is brightest on axis, a large share of the light leaves at oblique angles, so lenses or reflectors are used to gather it when a narrow area must be lit. The intensity falls to half its on-axis value at 60°, giving a 120° full beam angle.

led-display-027.question: A display's screen luminance varies with the input code value V (0 to 1) as L = V^2.2 (with white luminance taken as 1). Roughly what percentage of the white luminance is shown when a gray of V = 0.5 is displayed?
choices: About 22%
About 50%
About 73%
led-display-027.explanation: L = 0.5^2.2 = exp(2.2 × ln0.5) ≈ 0.218, about 22%. About 50% assumes the luminance is proportional to the code value and ignores the gamma characteristic. About 73% is 0.5^(1/2.2), the code value needed for 50% luminance, worked backward. The eye is more sensitive to luminance differences at the dark end, so assigning code values by such a power law rather than in proportion to luminance keeps steps in the shadows from being visible even with a limited number of bits. Images are encoded with the inverse characteristic (about the 1/2.2 power), so the original brightness ratios are reproduced from capture through display.

led-display-028.question: In a top-emitting OLED, which emits through its top surface, the organic layers sit between a highly reflective bottom electrode and a semitransparent metal top electrode, forming a weak optical cavity (microcavity). Which statement correctly describes the effect of this structure?
choices: The cavity does not change the emission wavelength, so the spectrum is the same face-on and at an angle, and the only effect is uniform dimming from absorption in the top electrode
Light at the resonant wavelength is enhanced forward and the spectrum narrows, but viewed at an angle the resonance shifts to shorter wavelengths and the color changes
The resonance prevents light from leaving straight ahead and sends it out only at oblique angles, so the on-axis luminance drops and the panel looks brighter from the side
led-display-028.explanation: Light bouncing between the two electrodes adds up at wavelengths for which the round-trip phase is a multiple of 2π. Matching the layer thickness to the emission wavelength sends that light strongly forward, narrowing the spectrum and raising color purity. For light traveling at an angle, the round-trip path phase shrinks in proportion to cosθ, so the resonance moves to shorter wavelengths and the color and brightness change with viewing angle. The claim that the cavity affects neither wavelength nor direction is wrong; reduced forward emission happens only when the thickness misses the resonance condition. In real panels the organic thickness is varied for each color of subpixel to balance on-axis efficiency against the color shift with angle.

led-display-029.question: In a VA (vertical alignment) liquid crystal display, the liquid crystal molecules stand perpendicular to the substrates when no voltage is applied, and the cell sits between two polarizers with crossed transmission axes. Which statement correctly describes this mode?
choices: With no voltage the molecules rotate the polarization by 90° and the pixel is white; applying voltage stands the molecules up and gives black, so it is a normally white mode
Birefringence is greatest when the molecules are perpendicular to the substrates, changing the polarization most, so the pixel is brightest without voltage and black is shown by applying voltage
With vertical molecules, light arriving face-on sees no birefringence and keeps its polarization, so the pixel is black without voltage and deep blacks and high contrast are easy to obtain
led-display-029.explanation: Light traveling along the long axis of the liquid crystal molecules experiences no birefringence, so when the molecules stand perpendicular to the substrates, face-on light keeps its polarization and is blocked by the crossed polarizers, giving black (normally black). Applying voltage tilts the molecules, birefringence appears, the polarization changes, and light passes. Because little light leaks in the black state, higher contrast ratios are easier to reach than with TN or IPS. Rotating the polarization by 90° to give white is the normally white operation of TN. Saying birefringence is greatest with vertical molecules has it backwards. Viewed obliquely, birefringence appears even in the black state and leakage grows, so pixels are divided into domains of different orientation or compensated with retardation films.

led-display-030.question: What is the main reason for building an LED's active region as a double heterostructure, in which a thin layer with a small band gap (a quantum well) is sandwiched between layers with a larger band gap?
choices: The injected electrons and holes are confined in the thin layer at high density, speeding up radiative recombination, and the outer layers barely absorb the emitted light, so the efficiency rises
The wide-gap outer layers set the emission wavelength, so the color can be chosen freely by the composition of the outer layers alone without changing the active material
The extra junctions lower the forward voltage, so less power is needed for the same current, and the efficiency rises even though the radiative recombination rate is unchanged
led-display-030.explanation: The rate of radiative recombination is roughly proportional to the product of the electron and hole densities. When a small-gap layer is sandwiched between larger-gap layers, the injected carriers cannot cross the barriers and are confined in the thin layer; their density rises and they recombine quickly, which helps radiative recombination win over nonradiative recombination at defects. The outer layers also have band gaps larger than the photon energy, so they hardly absorb the light, making it easier to extract. The emission wavelength is set mainly by the band gap of the confining layer and the well thickness, not chosen by the outer layers. Adding junctions does not lower the forward voltage and is not the source of the efficiency gain.

led-display-031.question: Which value is closest to the pixel density (pixels per inch, ppi) of a 27-inch-diagonal display (1 inch = 25.4 mm) with 3840 × 2160 pixels? Assume square pixels.
choices: About 163 ppi
About 142 ppi
About 64 ppi
led-display-031.explanation: The diagonal pixel count is √(3840² + 2160²) ≈ 4406, and dividing by the 27-inch diagonal gives about 163 ppi. The pixel pitch is 25.4/163 ≈ 0.156 mm. About 142 ppi divides the 3840 horizontal pixels by the diagonal; the horizontal count must be divided by the width, about 23.5 inches for a 16:9 screen. About 64 divides the diagonal pixel count by the diagonal in centimeters (about 68.6 cm), which is pixels per centimeter. For the same pixel count a smaller screen has a higher density, and smartphones viewed close to the eye use several hundred ppi.

led-display-032.question: On a hold-type display that refreshes at 60 Hz and keeps each frame on screen until the next one, an object moves horizontally at 960 pixels per second and is followed by the eye. Which value is closest to the width of the blur seen as the image smears across the retina? (Assume the pixel response is fast enough.)
choices: About 1 pixel
About 8 pixels
About 16 pixels
led-display-032.explanation: The eye tracks the object smoothly, so the gaze moves 960/60 = 16 pixels during one frame. Meanwhile the image stays lit at the same place on the screen, so it smears 16 pixels across the retina and appears as about 16 pixels of blur. Even with fast pixels, this blur remains as long as the display holds each image. About 1 pixel assumes that blur depends only on pixel response speed. About 8 pixels is what you get by raising the refresh rate to 120 Hz or by inserting black to halve the lit time of each frame. Black-frame insertion and strobed backlights reduce motion blur precisely by shortening this hold time.

led-display-033.question: LEDs are usually driven by a circuit that regulates the current (constant-current drive) rather than by a fixed voltage. Which is the main reason?
choices: An LED behaves like a resistor whose current is proportional to voltage, so with the current fixed, brightness can be finely adjusted by the square of the voltage
Current rises exponentially with voltage and, at a fixed voltage, increases with temperature, so voltage drive lets the current vary widely and invites thermal runaway
LED light is proportional to the number of photons at a wavelength set by the voltage, so constant current keeps the wavelength fixed while brightness is adjusted by the voltage
led-display-033.explanation: LED current follows the diode equation I ∝ exp(qV/(nkT)) and changes exponentially with voltage, so a small voltage difference causes a large change in current. Moreover, the forward voltage at a given current falls as the temperature rises (so at a given voltage the current increases); with a fixed voltage, heating raises the current, which raises the temperature further, and thermal runaway can result. Device-to-device variations in forward voltage also make the brightness uneven. Because the light output is roughly proportional to the current (the number of injected electrons), regulating the current stabilizes the brightness. Treating the LED as a resistor proportional to voltage is wrong; the wavelength is set mainly by the band gap, and brightness is not adjusted by voltage in this scheme.

led-display-034.question: InGaN blue LEDs usually have a thin AlGaN layer with a larger band gap between the active region (quantum wells) and the p-type layers. Which is the main role of this layer (the electron-blocking layer)?
choices: It forms a high conduction-band barrier that stops electrons from overshooting the active region into the p side, so more of them recombine in the active region
As a low-index layer, it totally reflects light from the active region back toward the substrate at the interface, raising the light-extraction efficiency from the top surface
It blocks holes coming from the p-type layer so fewer enter the active region, balancing the numbers of holes and electrons and thereby suppressing efficiency droop
led-display-034.explanation: Electrons have higher mobility and smaller effective mass than holes, so they tend to pass over the quantum wells without being captured and leak into the p side. Electrons that recombine on the p side give no light, lowering the injection efficiency and contributing to efficiency droop at high current. The AlGaN electron-blocking layer forms a high conduction-band barrier that stops this leakage and keeps electrons in the active region. Blocking holes as well would starve the active region of holes and backfire, so the valence-band barrier is designed to be as small as possible. The layer is only a few tens of nanometers thick and is not intended to confine light or reflect it back by total reflection.

led-display-035.question: In a liquid-crystal display, slow liquid-crystal response when switching from one gray level to another blurs moving images and leaves trails. Which describes the idea of overdrive, used to improve this?
choices: Turn the backlight off once in the middle of each frame to hide the light while the liquid crystal switches, eliminating the response delay itself
Apply a larger voltage than the target in the first frame of the transition only, so the molecules move faster and reach the target transmittance sooner
Pass a large current through each pixel to heat the liquid crystal and lower its viscosity, keeping the molecular rotation fast at all times
led-display-035.explanation: How fast the liquid-crystal molecules reorient is set by the torque from the electric field (the applied voltage) and by the viscosity, and transitions between nearby gray levels tend to be slow. Overdrive looks at the previous and next gray levels and, for the first frame only, applies a voltage larger (or smaller) than the target value, driving the molecules faster so the target transmittance is approached within one frame. The voltages are taken from a lookup table for each pair of levels to avoid overshoot. Turning the backlight off (black insertion) is a different method that makes the delay less visible but does not remove it. A liquid crystal reorients in an electric field; it is not heated by passing current.

led-display-036.question: In an IPS liquid-crystal pixel, treat the liquid-crystal layer with voltage applied as a uniform retarder whose slow axis is at 45° to the transmission axes of the two crossed polarizers. Which value is closest to the smallest liquid-crystal layer thickness d that maximizes the transmittance T ∝ sin²(πΔn d/λ) at 550 nm (liquid-crystal birefringence Δn = 0.10)?
choices: About 2.75 µm
About 1.38 µm
About 5.50 µm
led-display-036.explanation: sin²(πΔn d/λ) reaches its maximum of 1 when πΔn d/λ = π/2, that is, Δn d = λ/2: the layer acts as a half-wave plate, rotating the incident linear polarization by 90° so that it passes the exit polarizer. Then d = λ/(2Δn) = 0.550 µm/(2 × 0.10) = 2.75 µm. About 1.38 µm assumes Δn d = λ/4; the layer then acts as a quarter-wave plate producing circular polarization, and the transmission is only half the maximum. About 5.50 µm assumes Δn d = λ; the polarization returns to its original state and no light passes. In a real pixel the orientation is not uniform through the thickness, so Δn d is chosen somewhat larger than this, and because the optimum depends on wavelength, it is matched near green, where the eye is most sensitive.

led-display-037.question: A display of 3840 × 2160 pixels, each made of three micro-LEDs (red, green and blue), is assembled. If each micro-LED chip is transferred correctly to the substrate with a probability of 99.99%, which value is closest to the expected number of defective chips in one panel?
choices: About 830
About 25,000
About 2,500
led-display-037.explanation: There are 3840 × 2160 × 3 ≈ 2.49×10⁷ chips, and the defect probability per chip is 1 − 0.9999 = 1×10⁻⁴, so the expected number of defects is 2.49×10⁷ × 10⁻⁴ ≈ 2,500. About 830 forgets the factor of three for red, green and blue and counts only pixels; about 25,000 takes the defect probability as 10⁻³, one order too large. Even with a yield as high as 99.99%, handling tens of millions of chips leaves thousands of defects, so micro-LED displays need a repair step after transfer: lighting tests followed by replacing defective chips or providing spare chips. The more pixels and the smaller the chips, the heavier this transfer and repair burden becomes.

led-display-038.question: In OLED displays, showing the same image for a long time, such as a clock or a screen frame, can leave its shape visible afterward ("burn-in"). Which is the main cause?
choices: Liquid-crystal molecules held in one orientation for long become fixed to the alignment layer and no longer return when the voltage changes
Each pixel's luminance falls with drive current times time, so only pixels that shone brightly for long dim
The pixels' emitting materials have long afterglow, so the same shape keeps glowing for a while after the image changes
led-display-038.explanation: In an OLED pixel, the organic materials degrade gradually with the amount of charge passed (current times time), and the luminance at a given current falls. Only the pixels that displayed bright content for a long time dim faster, so when the image changes their shape shows up as nonuniformity. The degradation rate differs by color, and blue materials in particular have short lifetimes, so the color balance also shifts. Countermeasures include shifting the image slightly over time, compensating the current based on estimated aging, enlarging the emitting area to lower the current density, and tandem structures with stacked emitting units that need less current for the same luminance. Alignment that fails to recover is image retention in liquid-crystal displays, and OLEDs contain no liquid crystal. Afterglow would leave a bright image, the opposite of burn-in, which remains dark.

led-display-039.question: In a liquid-crystal display, the time for the molecules to return to their original orientation after the voltage is switched off (the relaxation response time) is τ ≈ γd²/(Kπ²) for a layer of thickness d, where γ is the rotational viscosity and K the elastic constant. Which correctly describes making the layer thinner to speed up the response?
choices: Halving the thickness cuts the response time to about 1/4, but a liquid crystal with larger birefringence Δn is then needed to keep Δn d unchanged
Halving the thickness cuts the response time to about 1/2, and the transmittance does not change even though Δn d shrinks, so the same material works
The response time depends only on viscosity, not thickness, so to speed it up a reverse voltage is applied instead of switching the voltage off
led-display-039.explanation: The relaxation after switch-off is set by the balance between the elastic restoring force from the alignment layers and the rotational viscosity, so τ is proportional to d². Halving the thickness reduces the response time to (1/2)² = 1/4. However, the pixel transmission is set by the retardation Δn d, so keeping, for example, Δn d = λ/2 requires a liquid crystal with correspondingly larger Δn. Materials with large Δn also tend to be more viscous, so the material combination is optimized. Making the response time proportional to d gives 1/2, which overlooks the square in the formula. The option that it does not depend on thickness contradicts the formula. The torque on the liquid crystal is proportional to the square of the field, so a reverse voltage cannot push the molecules back.

led-display-040.question: Placing a reflective polarizer film (a birefringent multilayer that transmits one polarization and reflects the orthogonal one) between the backlight and the lower polarizer of a liquid-crystal display makes the screen brighter. Which correctly explains why?
choices: The reflective film absorbs no light, so all light entering the polarizer has the transmitted polarization and the lower polarizer can be omitted
The multilayer reinforces light of particular wavelengths by interference, so the intensity of the transmitted polarization itself doubles
The polarization that an absorbing polarizer would discard is reflected back into the backlight, where diffusion and reflection change it for reuse
led-display-040.explanation: When unpolarized backlight passes an absorbing polarizer, about half of it, the orthogonal polarization, is absorbed and turned into heat. A reflective polarizer film instead reflects this polarization back toward the backlight without absorbing it. As the returned light is scattered and reflected by the diffuser and reflector, its polarization state changes, and part of it becomes the transmitted polarization and passes the film on a later pass; repeated round trips recycle the light and brighten the screen for the same power. Not all of it is converted and some is absorbed along the way, so the gain falls short of a factor of two. The light passing the film is not polarized well enough, so the absorbing polarizer is kept to maintain contrast. Interference does not increase the light intensity itself.

led-display-041.question: The forward voltage of a blue LED, measured with a small, short-pulsed measuring current (1 mA), is 3.100 V at a junction temperature of 25 °C, with a temperature coefficient of −2.0 mV/K. Right after operating the LED at high current until its temperature settles, the current is switched to the same 1 mA and the voltage is 3.020 V. Which combination of method and value for the junction temperature is correct?
choices: About −15 °C: the forward voltage dropped, so the junction is concluded to be colder than the 25 °C of the calibration
About 65 °C: the 80 mV drop measured at the same small current as used for the calibration is divided by the temperature coefficient, giving a 40 K rise
About 65 °C: no need to switch to the measuring current; just convert the forward voltage at the high operating current with the same coefficient
led-display-041.explanation: The temperature change is (3.020 − 3.100) V / (−2.0 mV/K) = +40 K, so the junction temperature is 25 + 40 = 65 °C. A higher temperature narrows the band gap and lowers the voltage needed for the same current, so the coefficient is negative. Concluding that the junction cooled because the voltage fell reverses this sign. At high current the forward voltage includes the drop across the series resistance and changes with temperature differently from the low-current value, so the current must be switched to the same small calibration current and measured within microseconds, before the junction cools. Junction temperature strongly affects lifetime, efficiency, and wavelength, so this is used to check thermal design.

led-display-042.question: A smartphone screen is viewed from 30 cm. Taking as the guide for pixels becoming indistinguishable the pixel spacing at which one pixel subtends 1 arcminute (1/60°) at the eye, which value is closest to the corresponding pixel density (pixels per inch, 1 inch = 25.4 mm, ppi)?
choices: About 11 ppi
About 580 ppi
About 290 ppi
led-display-042.explanation: The pixel spacing corresponding to 1 arcminute is 300 mm × tan(1/60°) ≈ 300 mm × 2.91×10⁻⁴ ≈ 0.087 mm, so per inch it is 25.4/0.087 ≈ 291, about 290 ppi. About 11 ppi stops at 1/0.087 ≈ 11.5, which is pixels per millimeter, not converted to inches. About 580 ppi treats 1 arcminute as one period of a pattern made of a light and a dark pixel, making each pixel 0.5 arcminute. The guide for visual resolution is inversely proportional to viewing distance, so for a TV or monitor viewed from 60 cm, pixels become hard to see at half that, about 145 ppi. Actual perception also depends on brightness, contrast, and individual visual acuity.

led-display-043.question: The transmittance of a 90°-twisted TN liquid-crystal cell (no voltage) placed between two crossed polarizers is T = 1 − sin²((π/2)√(1 + u²))/(1 + u²), with u = 2Δn d/λ (the Gooch–Tarry formula). For Δn = 0.10 and λ = 550 nm, which value is closest to the thinnest cell thickness d giving T = 1?
choices: About 4.8 µm
About 2.8 µm
About 10.7 µm
led-display-043.explanation: T = 1 when sin²((π/2)√(1 + u²)) = 0, that is, when √(1 + u²) = 2, 4, …; the first condition is u = √3. Then d = √3λ/(2Δn) = 1.732 × 0.55 µm/(2 × 0.10) ≈ 4.76 µm, about 4.8 µm. About 2.8 µm applies the half-wave condition of an untwisted plate, Δn d = λ/2; this gives u = 1 and a transmittance of only about 68%. About 10.7 µm is the next condition, u = √15; it also gives T = 1 but is not the thinnest thickness. A thicker cell makes the polarization follow the twist more reliably, but the liquid crystal's response time grows with the square of the thickness, so the thickness of the first condition is used.

led-display-044.question: In one type of liquid-crystal display, the field-sequential method, no color filters are used; red, green, and blue backlights flash in turn within each frame, and the liquid crystal displays the image for each color in sync. Which feature of this method is correct?
choices: Each pixel emits the three colors at the same time, so the liquid crystal may respond slowly, and colors never appear separated when the eyes or objects move
With no color filters, light efficiency rises, but each color needs separate pixels, so the resolution drops to one third
It avoids discarding about two thirds of the light in color filters, but the liquid crystal must switch three times faster, and color breakup is easily seen
led-display-044.explanation: In a color-filter display, each pixel is divided into red, green, and blue subpixels, and each subpixel absorbs and discards about two thirds of the white light. In the field-sequential method, every pixel passes the current backlight color directly, so light efficiency rises, and the same number of liquid-crystal pixels gives three times the resolution. In exchange, even for a 60 Hz display the colors are shown in turn, so the liquid crystal needs a fast response to switch at 180 Hz or more. And because the colors are separated in time, when the eyes or objects move the color images shift on the retina, and rainbow-like colors appear at edges (color breakup). The claim that the three colors are emitted simultaneously overlooks that this method separates them in time.

led-display-045.question: Deep-ultraviolet AlGaN LEDs at 260–280 nm have external quantum efficiencies much lower than blue InGaN LEDs, often only a few percent. Which combination of main reasons is correct?
choices: AlGaN approaches an indirect-gap semiconductor as its Al content rises, so radiative recombination needs phonons to supply momentum, and the internal quantum efficiency is inherently low
Al-rich layers give poor p-type conduction and hole injection, and the UV-absorbing p-GaN contact and a polarization that hardly escapes the surface hurt extraction
The sapphire substrate strongly absorbs ultraviolet light shorter than 280 nm, so light cannot be extracted through the substrate side and most of the light going out is lost
led-display-045.explanation: AlGaN has a direct gap at all compositions, so an indirect gap is not the cause. In Al-rich AlGaN, the magnesium acceptor level used for p-type doping is deep and few holes are produced, so a p-GaN layer is added on the contact side to conduct current; but GaN, with a band gap of about 3.4 eV (about 365 nm), absorbs deep-UV light. In addition, at high Al content the emission becomes mainly polarized with its electric field parallel to the crystal c axis, so light tends to travel along the plane and is hard to extract through the c-plane surface. High dislocation densities also lower the internal quantum efficiency. Sapphire has a band gap of about 9 eV and is transparent in the deep UV, so flip-chip structures that emit through the substrate side are commonly used.
